title: Something Is Changing in How Nigerians See a Dog
body:
For a long time, the default job for a dog in a lot of Nigerian homes was security: feed it, keep it in the compound, let it bark at strangers. That hasn't disappeared, but it is no longer the whole story. The Guardian ran a piece this year with a small, telling detail: people now stop on the street to ask a dog's name, and even reach down to stroke it, something that would have looked unusual not long ago.

It isn't just a stray observation. Punch recently ran a column by pet advocate Oga Duke making a related case, arguing for pets to be treated as closer to family than to property. We haven't read either piece in full and won't pretend to summarize their arguments beyond what the headlines say, but the fact that two separate outlets are running this conversation at all says something: this shift is real enough now to write about, not just a handful of individual households.

It's also the reason a site like PetMatch has any reason to exist. If a dog or cat is purely functional, there's little need to find it a mate, a playmate, or an owner nearby to compare notes with. But the moment a pet starts feeling like part of the household, people start caring about the things functional ownership never asked for: who else nearby has one like mine, is this actually a good match, what does the owner three streets over do differently.

That's a small, specific thing to build for, and we've tried to keep it that way. PetMatch doesn't charge for listings or matches, doesn't take a cut of anything you work out with another owner, and doesn't independently verify what anyone writes in their listing beyond what they tell us. What it can do is make the first connection easier, so the actual decision, the WhatsApp conversation, the meeting, the question about temperament or vaccination history, happens between two real owners instead of a forwarded number or a random Facebook comment.

If the culture really is moving toward treating pets as part of the family, the ordinary infrastructure around that, vets, breeders, boarding, and a directory or two, has some catching up to do. Worth doing carefully rather than quickly: before meeting anyone to arrange a mating or a playdate, it's worth reading through how to do that safely at https://petmatch.fit/safety.
link_label: The Guardian: Nigerians embrace dogs as pets
